opus-5.5.text:
I think this is actually the most essential nature of the whole thing. When you work on AI, you never really arrive at a state where everything is solved and you can just rest. Every time you push the capability one step further, you open up a new frontier, and that frontier exposes problems you couldn't even see before.

There's a way of thinking I find quite useful, which is that new problems are not a sign that something went wrong. They're a sign that you've made progress. If you're still stuck on the same old problems, that's when you should worry. For example, a few years ago the core question was whether models could even produce fluent, coherent language. Once that was largely solved by scaling, the problem became reasoning: can the model think through multiple steps? Then once reasoning improved, you start caring about long context, about agents, about whether the model can actually take actions in the real world over a long horizon. And then you hit questions about data, because high-quality data on the internet is finite, so how do you keep scaling? Each layer only becomes visible after you climb the previous one.

So I tend to see it as a kind of infinite game. The important thing isn't to eliminate problems, but to make sure you're always working on the right ones, the problems that sit at the most important bottleneck at that moment. A lot of the job, especially for a company, is judgment: among all the new problems that appear, which ones are fundamental and which ones are just noise or engineering details that will be solved naturally later.

And I think there's also something philosophically interesting here. In a sense, AI is a process of converting energy and compute into intelligence, and intelligence itself is about solving problems. So it makes sense that as the system gets smarter, the problems also get more interesting. If the problems ever stopped emerging, it might mean we had hit a ceiling. I'd much rather live in a world where the questions keep getting harder, because that means the space of what's possible is still expanding.

Personally, I find that quite exciting rather than frustrating. It's what keeps the work meaningful. You have to stay humble, because whatever you think is the final answer today will probably look naive in a year or two. But that's exactly the fun of it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the emergence of new problems is actually the most natural thing in the world when you're working on AI. It's not an accident, and it's not a sign that something has gone wrong. It's the shape of the work itself.

When we started, the problem was fairly clear: can we get a model to learn language well enough to be useful? Then you solve some version of that, and immediately the answer opens up ten new questions. How do you make it reason rather than just imitate? How do you get it to use tools, to act in the world, to remember things across a long horizon? Each answer raises the ceiling, and the moment the ceiling rises you see a whole new layer of problems you literally couldn't see before, because you weren't tall enough to look over the edge.

So I've stopped thinking of new problems as obstacles. I think of them as evidence of progress. If we ever hit a point where no new problems appeared, that would worry me much more, because it would mean we'd stopped moving.

The second thing I'd say is that a lot of these problems are not really "new" in the deepest sense. Many of them are old questions wearing new clothes. How do you generalize from limited data? How do you balance exploration and exploitation? How do you align what a system optimizes for with what you actually want? These questions existed before deep learning. What changes is the scale and the concrete form they take. So part of the skill is recognizing when a problem that looks unprecedented is actually a familiar one at a new scale, and when it genuinely is something nobody has faced before.

And the third thing, which is maybe more personal: I think you have to hold two attitudes at the same time. One is a kind of first-principles ambition, where you believe the big problems are solvable and you keep pushing toward them. The other is humility about timelines and about your own current understanding. Almost every time we've been confident about exactly how something would unfold, reality has been a bit different. Scaling laws held in ways some people doubted, but the specific capabilities that emerged surprised almost everyone, including the people doing the scaling.

So how do I understand the continual emergence of new problems? I'd say: it's the frontier being honest with you. It's telling you where you actually are. And the right response isn't to feel overwhelmed by it. It's to pick the problem that matters most right now, that's barely within reach, and go after it with everything you have, knowing that solving it will show you the next one.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a natural part of developing AI. When you solve one problem, you expand what the system can do, and that exposes problems you couldn’t really see before. A model becomes better at answering individual questions, for example, and you start asking whether it can complete a longer task reliably. Then maintaining context, correcting mistakes, and knowing when to stop become much more important.

So I wouldn’t measure progress by whether new problems stop appearing. I’d ask whether the problems are changing because we’ve overcome earlier limitations. At the same time, we have to distinguish between fixing a particular failure and addressing the underlying cause. Otherwise, we can spend all our time patching examples without making the system fundamentally better.

For me, that’s the research process: use the problems we encounter to question our assumptions, identify the most important bottleneck, and decide what to try next.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a natural part of developing AI. When you solve one problem, you expand what the system can do, and that exposes limitations you couldn’t see before. A model becomes better at answering questions, and then you start asking whether it can reason reliably, handle longer tasks, or recognize when it’s wrong.

So I don’t expect there to be a point where all the problems disappear. The important thing is whether we’re making progress on the underlying capabilities, and whether the new problems help us understand what’s still missing. You have to keep moving between concrete experiments and the bigger question of what principles will let these systems improve.
